It defines a measure called 'future accuracy potential' as a theoretical limit of a stream's classification accuracy beyond the present data set, achieved by adapting decision trees to include relevant features from the entire data stream. This concept drives the development of a method to estimate a stream's future accuracy potential, resulting in superior classification performance when compared to other existing algorithms on diverse data streams. Furthermore, the proposed approach outperforms benchmark models in both online and offline evaluation scenarios, according to evaluation results based on well-known data streams. Additionally, the method exhibits desirable density and scalability properties, thus facilitating easier interpretation of its results. To expand upon this found potential, we also investigate ways to adapt features to a stream's evolving structure during the classification process. This investigation enables features to be extracted more accurately and naturally, leading to improved classification performance and more coherent, interpretable models. Finally, the paper explores how to extend the methodology to handle missing values in the data stream, thus further enhancing the estimation of a stream's future accuracy potential. Experiments on diverse data streams from various sources have validated the reliability of the proposed approach. Specifically, we establish that every conformal submersion metric meets the criteria for a Landau metric, and vice versa.  Additionally, we identify key characteristics that define conformal submersion metrics and use these to create a simple test for determinism in the concept.  Furthermore, we establish a method for determining all possible conformal submersion metrics on a given manifold by specifying an arbitrary real-valued function and then using a consistent projection technique to generate the metric.  This approach is pivotal in addressing the decisive question of whether a general Landau metric can be classified as a conformal submersion metric.  Ultimately, we devise a specific criteria set for a Landau metric to conformally submersive and prove that any metric meeting these criteria will indeed be a conformal submersion metric.  This conclusion is key to resolving an existing open issue in the field.  In the course of our research, we also accidentally stumble upon a novel characterization of conformal submersion metrics, which we then use to confirm that a general Landau metric and a conformally flat submersion metric are mutually exclusive concepts.  Lastly, we take a closer look at the properties of a specific interaction between two manifolds - as one undergoes a conformal submersion - and finds that its associated tangential bundle will meet the criteria for a certain metric condition, ultimately being redefined as a particular type of Riemannian submersion metric, with a specific relationship to the original conformal submersion metric, allowing for an easy translation between the two.  This research also leads to a new theory regarding the relationship between two types of metrics - a Poincaré-Adams type, and a Laptev type - and finds a specific condition under which they will be equivalent, with this condition also defining a specific type of conformal submersion metric.  This new theorem also holds true for a specific type of metric, known as a Landau metric, and also leads to a determination of the general conformal submersion metric, with its associated scalar curvature polynomial being explicitly defined. We derive the Weyl curvature term's impact on the purity loss of a quantum state in a classical gravity setting. Furthermore, our analysis extends this concept to investigate the purity loss in a quantum field theory context as a function of the Weyl curvature's complex part. Ultimately, our study explores the purity loss's potential as a tool for observing Weyl curvature effects. We conclude that such an approach may not be highly effective due to the pure state's rapid return to its ground state. Nevertheless, this research opens the door for future research on Weyl curvature effects in quantum gravity. Our work further reveals that the purity loss is related to the second coefficient ($\beta_2$) of the Weyl curvature expansion and that this relationship holds not only in de Sitter but also in any other spacetime with a constant curvature. Additionally, our study shows that the purity loss can be expressed solely in terms of the trace of the square of a quantum field's operator, a finding that may have implications for future observational studies. Ultimately, our work links the purity loss to the quantum gravity phase shift and suggests that this effect could be tested with relatively simple measurements, a single spin-0 field and a single fermion field. The purity loss we derive here is a universal property of the Weyl curvature's impact on quantum gravity, a feature we hope will be useful in developing future research on this effect. Our work here represents the first investigation of the purity loss in a quantum gravity setting and suggests that this effect could be used in future observations of Weyl curvature effects. Our study also shows that the purity loss can be used to distinguish between quantum gravity and a quantum non-gravitational field theory. This study explores the primary dependence of principal component dynamics (PRC) in dual-support walking humans.  PRC serves as a useful tool for reducing high-dimensional data while identifying time-series patterns, and is particularly useful for non-stationary signals like human walking.  Notably, the application of PRC to walking data highlights two distinct states characterized by differing levels of lower limb movement: a state with prominent higher-frequencies and a state with predominant lower frequencies.  Although the underlying mechanisms for these states are not yet fully understood, the higher-frequency state may be associated with voluntary control, while the lower-frequency state could be attributed to involuntary movements.  The majority of PRC values for walking were found to be centered around their mean values, with significant variations in the proportions of doublets, triplets, and quadruplets, especially in the higher-frequency state.  Furthermore, PRC's potential to capture asymmetries in walking gait was confirmed, and its potential to serve as a control signal for prosthetic devices was also investigated.  The study provides theoretical foundations for using PRC in walking analysis, and paves the way for future studies on this topic. Our analysis reveals dynamic connections among the variables and particularly notes that migration rates often reflect reflections of underlying trends in population changes and fertility behaviors, while fertility and mortality rates exhibit more independent patterns.  Although there are noticeable differences between Europe and South Asia in their population dynamics, both regions share a common thread of evolving trends driven by shifting social norms, urbanization, education levels, and economic development.  Our study demonstrates the benefits of jointly modeling multiple demographic variables to uncover their interplay and unique characteristics.  Our method provides a versatile tool for exploring the interplay of demographic variables and the evolution of population dynamics.  Our data covers a period of 60 years, spanning from 1950 to 2010, and is based on seven regularly collected census and national statistics data sets. of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) can be accurately predicted using a simple mathematical model that accounts for the passage of time and takes into account changes in the emission of multiple bands. This approach allows for the conversion of UV data into standard wavelengths, rendering overall trends independent of time. By using this method with data collected from space observations, we can focus on variations in the optical and near-UV regions, which often exhibit different behaviors. On average, these regions move in opposite directions in response to changes in the overall UV emission. This phenomenon is observed in approximately half of the well-reported AGNs. Exceptions to this rule include Seyfert galaxies, the narrow-line quasars, and a subset of broad-line quasars. These exceptions are typically characterized by relatively low levels of variability. On the other hand, the highest variability is seen in the far-UV data of the most luminous quasars, with a notable exception being the significant 1963-1966 outburst of QSO 095012. This phenomenon is often associated with an overall increase in UV emission across multiple bands. Interestingly, the amplitude of these variations decreases as the wavelength increases, with this trend being most pronounced in the rest-frame ultraviolet. A possible interpretation of these findings is that the primary source of variability is the changes in the UV radiation's source itself, with the timing and extent of these changes associated with the time it takes for information to travel between the source and the observation point. This could also explain the observed correlation between UV emission and lag, known as the "echo effect." Furthermore, we found that this simple mathematical model allows for the accurate prediction of optical and near-UV variations on time scales of thousands of days, with the associated lags being consistent with previous studies. Ultimately, the application of this model enables the identification of the UV sources of AGNs and contributes to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms behind their variability. in spatially-resolved spectra of the planetary nebulae (PNe) in the Galaxy centre, taking into account their asymmetrical morphology. These findings are based on the full spectral analysis of high-quality IFU data, previously collected by the MUSE instrument as part of a larger survey. This survey covers a significant portion of the Galaxy's disc and out to a distance of 10 kpc. We define an asymmetry measure for line intensity, accounting for the nebula's radius and brightness. These calculations demonstrate that the asymmetry of the emission line [Ne III] lambda 3862 is greater in the outer regions of the PNe. Conversely, the emission line [O III] lambda 5007 exhibits greater asymmetry in the inner regions. We have determined a linear relationship between the line asymmetry and the nebula radius, taking into account factors like the ionization density and the gas flow speed. Additionally, we find a link between the line asymmetry and the nebula's density, with higher ionization densities corresponding to greater asymmetry. By analysing the line asymmetry as a characteristic property of the PNe, we can better understand the gas outflow speed and ionization density, thus refining the classification of the PNe in the Galaxy. Furthermore, we find that the line asymmetry can act as a proxy for the ionization density, with certain limitations. This study investigates the presence of bias in machine learning models, particularly those that rely on probability distributions, by examining how conditional distributional assumptions affect predicted probabilities. Our analysis demonstrates that even when all other factors remain equal, models that sample from a posterior distribution are more susceptible to biases compared to deterministic models. We further note that addressing this bias will require more extensive training datasets, an increase in computational resources, and a more detailed understanding of the issues at hand. Our research is an evaluation of the potential for machine learning to address the problem, rather than a solution in and of itself. Ultimately, the potential for bias in machine learning models serves as a reminder that, when relying on these models, we must also consider the potential consequences of their output, rather than regarding them as an objective reality. Several practical strategies for dealing with bias in machine learning were discussed, including reducing the influence of probability sampling and using models that produce deterministic outcomes. By exploring the trade-offs involved, we can work towards creating models that not only provide accurate predictions but also mitigate potential biases. However, proving the integrity of these designs can be challenging because traditional methods rely on fixed sample sizes, making it difficult to apply them to adaptive designs.  Two notable Bayesian adaptive concepts, the Frequentist Equivalency Principle and the Bayesian Equivalency Framework, have been developed to assess the integrity of these designs, primarily by using asymptotic reasoning.  Unfortunately, this approach compromises individual trial integrity by assuming freedoms in the Frequentist Equivalency Principle and the Bayesian Equivalency Framework.  As an alternative, we propose adopting the Simple Random Sample (SRS) concept from the Frequentist framework to verify adaptive Bayesian design integrity, which we term Bayesian Integrity through SRS (BIST).  BIST is grounded in the fundamental principles of frequentism and does not grant freedoms.  We derive general requirements for verifying BIST and illustrate its applicability to commonly used Bayesian adaptive concepts, such as Bayesian adaptive enrollment and Bayesian withdrawal.  Through numerical simulations, we show that BIST successfully validates these adaptive designs, even at small sample sizes.  As a result, we recommend SRS as a gold standard for verifying the integrity of Bayesian adaptive designs.  Furthermore, we discover that popular software like R and Python's RStudio are incapable of producing valid SRS sequences, prompting us to create our own SRS generating tool.  We make this tool publicly available for the community to use.  Additionally, we provide a public repository containing our validation simulation code.  We hope that our work accelerates the verification of Bayesian adaptive design integrity and helps to establish a uniform set of rules for assessing these designs, ultimately enhancing the integrity of these designs in the eyes of the FDA.  We also aim to establish a new standard for evaluating Bayesian adaptive concepts.  We have made a commitment to update this tool to include additional designs and field any queries on this work at https://bist-tool.net. A widely used metric called Frechet distance measures the similarity between two distributions of images and is typically calculated using the mean and standard deviation of their distances.  However, this approach can be impractical, leading to inconsistent results.  An alternative method involves using the average distance of each image to its nearest neighbor within a specified threshold.  This technique has several advantages, including lower computational requirements and more accurate results, particularly for small datasets.  This average nearest neighbor frequency-based approach for calculating Frechet distance (FREQ) has been found to effectively replace traditional methods in image synthesis evaluation.  FREQ has also been modified to accommodate supervised learning scenarios, yielding superior results in comparison to established evaluation methods.  The proposed frequency-based approach has been publicly released on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/edf-statistics/freq_fn.  FREQ has been successfully used in evaluating the generative models SNGANs and SNDPMs on the LSUN church dataset.  The evaluation results for these models can be found on the GitHub repository mentioned above. When the entire boundary data is known, this problem is fully resolved and its solution does not depend on the length of time. However, when only a portion of the boundary data is controlled, the situation becomes more complex and we identify the necessary and sufficient conditions for complete boundary data recovery. A relatively understudied area is the preprocessing stage focused on grouping data points together that belong to the same underlying generative model. This work centers on learning the intrinsic clusters within complex dataset generations from a hidden Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). Current methods are inefficient because they rely on expensive sampling or assume impractical conditions. To address this, we introduce ClusterMix, a novel approach that uses an efficient sampling method to separate overlapping clusters. ClusterMix consists of two main models: a GMM that samples data points into distinct clusters and a clustering model that groups data points based on the density function estimated by the GMM. Through extensive testing, we demonstrate that ClusterMix surpasses previous methods, even those with performance guarantees, while also providing seamless interpretability of its clustering results. ClusterMix also effectively resolves issues associated with mode collapsing and performs well even when dataset data is limited or comes from a small number of components. To further enhance its performance, we develop a Bayesian version of ClusterMix that allows for the joint estimation of model parameters and the number of clusters. This Bayesian approach even accommodates cases where the clustering model assumes Dirichlet distribution on cluster assignments. The core Bayesian version is approximated using a variational lower bound (VB-ClusterMix), which utilizes adversarial training to obtain a reliable approximation. The computational efficiency of ClusterMix enables it to achieve competitive results on various benchmark datasets while also producing reliable insights into its training. Moreover, ClusterMix's performance is comparable to that of methods with performance guarantees, particularly on dataset generations from a single component GMM. In the cases where input data is structured, such as in the form of sequences or images with distinct regions, natural patterns of error occur during the autoencoding process. This error patterns often contain meaningful and interpretable information. Our method, which we refer to as the Structured Error Analysis (SEA), aims to uncover these patterns by quantifying the complexity of these errors based on the data's structural characteristics. In order to achieve this, SEA utilizes a set of intuitive metrics that evaluate error structure, and weighs them against an uncertainty threshold derived from the data's distribution. As a result, SEA not only identifies the second and third moments of the error distribution, but also generates an unsupervised structural code to characterize the nature of the errors that occur during the autoencoding process. The efficacy of our approach is showcased on a variety of experiments involving visual, linguistic, and biological data. analysis of the carbonization process of porous organic frameworks (POFs). This approach was tested using a sample material with known geometry and properties, and the results were compared with experimental findings. Carbonization in POFs involves the removal of volatiles and the connection of carbon atoms in a porous framework. To simplify the complex carbonization process, a model assumes uniform removal of volatiles and describes the carbon skeleton using the Kirchhoff-McShane algorithm. Based on this method, a linearized heat-diffusion equation and an elasticity problem are solved simultaneously to obtain the temperature distribution and the deformation of the porous material. Various parameters in the model are assumed to be temperature-dependent, following predetermined power-law functions. The model was validated by comparing the calculated pore sizes with the predicted pore diameters, and the results showed a reasonable correlation with the experimentally-measured pore sizes. Furthermore, a temperature distribution plot and the deformation of the material were visualized, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method in simulating the carbonization process of POFs. This approach can be applied to the analysis of carbonized porous materials with known geometries and properties. However, for materials with unknown internal structures, a reverse analysis can be employed to determine the material parameters and the pore geometry based on the experimental data and the carbonization model. This reverse problem will be the subject of further investigations. The carbonization model was also used to calculate the thermal conductivity of the carbonized material, and the results showed a reasonable correlation with the predicted conductivity. Finally, a demonstration demonstrated the capability of the carbonization model in simulating the carbonization of intricate materials with complex geometries. To this end, a mesh of a real-world material, known as MOF-505, was created and used in the carbonization analysis. Additionally, a plot of the thermal distribution within the material and the deformation of the material were provided, showcasing the effectiveness of the proposed method in analyzing carbonized porous materials. To confirm the applicability of the method, a demonstration was conducted on two diverse materials, a ship-shaped porous material and a material resembling skeletal muscle. This approach can be applied to the analysis of carbonized materials with any shape or geometry. Our proposed framework, Designed Distributed Decisions, aims to facilitate coordinated decision-making through a structured approach for distributed systems, ultimately ensuring seamless integration with real-time data and analytical models in the context of pandemic decision-making. This concept is successfully applied in the COVID-19 Technical advisory Group for Mexico (COTEMAC), where it supports the development of government policies.

This methodology features the breaking-down of complex problems into manageable parts, using specific analytical models to address each component, and implementing a formal decision-making process. This approach also involves using a dedicated platform to collect member inputs and display the results of all models in an integrated manner. 
  Our initial outcomes have led to the development of a fully-functional system that facilitates decision-making and produces consistent results. This system has been successfully applied in generating recommendations for vaccination and COVID-19 policy strategies. 
  However, we have identified some potential issues that may affect the long-term functionality of the solution, including ensuring member buy-in, addressing the ongoing development of the models, and implementing an efficient data governance policy. 
  Given that our framework has begun to demonstrate its value in supporting coordinated decision-making, we plan to continue refining it by gathering feedback from COTEMAC's members and exploring best practices in the development of analytical models.

A prominent challenge in developing these systems is often cited as the need for substantial amounts of data, yet in reality, most training parameters in neural networks typically remain unchanged. This presents an opportunity for optimization by highlighting wasteful computations and eliminating them. In response to this, a novel method called Neural Clean Lab (NCL) has been created with the primary objective of significantly reducing the time required to collect data by pinpointing and eliminating unnecessary neural computations. NCL achieves this by providing a dataflow graph visualization tool that allows users to manually intervene in the training process, identifying and eliminating redundant steps. Through experimentation on diverse workloads across computer vision and natural language processing domains, NCL has demonstrated the capability to accurately determine 57% of the redundant computations and successfully eliminated an average of 53% of the total parameters. Additionally, NCL in conjunction with autoML tools showed potential in enhancing the overall ML tuning process by boosting accuracy while cutting parameter reduction rates. Generally, it has been believed that the activity of a protein was solely dependent on its core protein structure along with the strength of its bound attachments. However, recent studies have demonstrated that the activity of a protein can also be influenced by its unbound protein regions through long-range interactions with other proteins. To gain a better understanding of this phenomenon and their effects on protein function, we have developed a computational model to analyze the effects of long-range interactions on a protein's activity levels. In our model, we used data from protein activity changes caused by single amino acid substitutions, taking into account the protein's entire sequence and its spatial structure across various distances. By applying this approach to a large dataset of protein activity changes, we have found that the protein regions with the highest activity-correlated signals are concentrated in the protein's surface areas and are significantly attached to other proteins. Notably, we found that a substantial proportion of these interacting regions are located at large distances from each other, exceeding 30 starch units in size. By leveraging our computational predictions, we have validated the actual protein experiments involving the ADAP2 and PIN1 proteins, which have demonstrated the importance of long-range interactions with a protein's surface regions for proper protein function. A notable example of a blockchain meeting this criterion is Probabilistic Differential Confidentiality (PDC), a blockchain variant that remains operational, albeit with reduced functionality, when up to $f$ out of $n$ nodes fail. Given the complexity of directly addressing failures in partial synchronous networks, this study focuses on developing a distributed algorithm for a PDC blockchain that includes the following key components: (a) constructing a complete graph of pairwise nodes within a $d$-dimensional space, (b) establishing a $(1-\frac{3}{2}f)$-secure majority consensus among participants, and (c) achieving an $8.5n^2$ time complexity for network coverage recovery after a failure event. The proposed approach employs a novel geometric voting mechanism to achieve these objectives. lecture notes from a course I taught at the University of Pennsylvania in the spring of 2022. The course, 'Random Matrices, Elliptic Operators and Inverse Problems,' is part of the prestigious PCMI graduate summer school. The diverse field of random matrix theory has significant connections to numerous other mathematical fields, particularly striking similarities in its outcomes and structures. 

  This set of notes focuses on three distinct topics: the first concerns the spectral theory of elliptic operators, the second explores the convergence of random matrices, and the third delves into inverse problems. Each of these topics has its own section, and while they can be read independently, they are designed to be read consecutively. 

  In the first section, we cover the measure-dependent Toda orbit, coalescence of eigenvalues, and the broad context of elliptic operators. In the second section, we delve into the band matrix approach, focusing on the solvability of the Schur flow and the second eigenvalue. In the third section, we undertake a comprehensive examination of inverse problems at a graduate level. 

  These lecture notes are intended for a diverse group of students. Some, like Yonatan Heimann, focused exclusively on the Schur flow, while others, such as Yangang Huang and Jiayang Liu, worked on the convergence of the eigenvalues of band random matrices, and others, like Shivan Khandani, explored the measure-dependent Toda orbit and the broad context of unimodular eigenvalue rigidity. I would especially like to acknowledge my collaborators, Ofer Zeitouni and Oleg Zariphopoulos, for their invaluable contributions to the notes. 

  It is my hope that these lecture notes will serve as a useful reference not just for the students who kindly agreed to contribute to their revision, but also for any other young mathematician who may find them helpful in their own research and educational pursuits. 

  I would be particularly grateful if you could cite the preprint version until the official release of the PCMI volume. 

  Please do not hesitate to reach out to me at szeitouni@univ-mail.univ-amman.ma or ozariph@univ-amman.ma with any inquiries.

However, determining the surface tension of small groups of particles when in contact with a liquid is a complex task due to the uncertainty in contact angle and particle size.  This led to the development of a new method utilizing X-ray free electron laser experiments to study the nucleation of water droplets in a vacuum. A three-dimensional, steady-state model employing the Navier-Stokes equations is used to investigate the flow within a diffuser-pump geometry. The computational domain is sectioned into several areas of varying complexity: a diffuser section with and without a heat transfer device, a helical ribbon impeller, a helical circular venturi, and a helical straight spiral membrane. Due to the high speeds at which the diffuser operates, Eulerian methods are often preferred over other methods. To evaluate the accuracy-complexity tradeoffs of the employed models, several approaches are compared. Notably, a low-order analytical model, the Widmann Diffuser Analysis Equation, is used to analyze the flow at a lower computational cost. Experimental testing confirms the computational findings, showcasing a 8% increase in diffuser efficiency when equipped with the heat transfer device. Furthermore, the results indicate that higher flow velocities within the diffuser can be achieved using the pin-fin heat transfer device, a crucial factor for pump performance. To optimize the design of this diffuser, a parametric study incorporating various pitch types and lengths of the pin-fins was conducted. Finally, the integration of the diffuser into a comprehensive pump model enabled the determination of the system's total efficiency when equipped with the enhanced diffuser. According to the calculations, the total system efficiency can be improved by a maximum of 2%. The primary factor contributing to this improvement is the reduced energy required due to the lower pressure needed to drive the pump, whereas the effect of the increased temperature on the pump's efficiency is minimal. Additionally, the total head and power that the pump needs to supply are reduced by 3% and 2%, respectively, when equipped with the diffuser. The findings of this study can provide valuable insights for designers and analysts working on pumps that operate under high temperatures. The computational models developed in this research can be easily adapted to analyze other types of diffusers and pumps. Furthermore, the methods employed and results obtained can be useful in guiding future research on this topic. The software used to conduct this analysis includes ANSYS Fluent for the fluid flow and heat transfer analysis, and SolidWorks for the geometric modeling, mesh creation, and assembly. Recent findings by Givran and Guan involve simplifications to the model, particularly in relation to the equivariant cohomology of complex nilpotent orbits. Our work here builds upon this by incorporating a notion of equivariant deformation quantization. This leads to a formulation of the tube structure in terms of a specific quantized symplectic geometry. Ultimately, this provides a way to compute the equivariant cohomology with characters instead of integers. The method is demonstrated specifically for the case of complex nilpotent orbits within the semisimple Lie algebras of types $B_n$, $C_n$, and $D_n$. The computations for $B_n$ were previously done by Givran; our work here reproduces those results while obtaining new results for $C_n$ and $D_n$. The method may also be applied more broadly to other types of orbits. However, the computation of equivariant cohomology with characters is generally a complex task, particularly for cases of simple orbits. An advantage of the tube structure is that it allows for the description of the equivariant cohomology with characters of the dual orbit by referring to the cohomology of the base $GL_{n+1}$, which is well-understood. This enables the representation-theoretic derivation of certain identities in harmonic analysis on nilpotent varieties, specifically the dual variety of a complex semisimple Lie algebra, which has been studied extensively. The identification of the equivariant cohomology with characters also allows for the description of the equivariant holomorphic Bott-Weil-type theorems for the cases of $C_n$ and $D_n$, which were previously only known with integers. The method employed here is also based on a certain formula expressing the equivariant cohomology with characters of the standard monomial differential as a result of the quantized symplectic geometry of a tube. Despite its prevalence, the impact of class imbalance on many machine learning problems remains poorly understood. In this review, we focus on supervised learning and delve into the causes and consequences of class imbalance. We also examine its effect on learning and predictability, as well as its impact when leveraging re-sampling methods, optimization techniques, and ensemble learning. Ultimately, our goal is to provide a thorough exploration of the interplay between class imbalance and machine learning. 

  The findings reveal that class imbalance can impede the performance of target variables and compromise the reliability of model training. However, certain problems are less affected by this issue. While attempts have been made to address class imbalance through data augmentation, design modifications, and performance metrics, more needs to be done. In fact, many deep learning models are capable of automatically mitigating the impact of class imbalance. Furthermore, the effect of class imbalance can be a double-edged sword, depending on the specific context. In addition, the consequences of misclassifying rare event instances are often more severe than misclassifying common event instances. In light of these findings, we propose the following areas for future research: developing more effective optimization techniques, adapting class imbalance handling to accommodate diverse dataset characteristics, and infusing domain knowledge into deep learning models to better handle class imbalance. Ultimately, our goal is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the intricate relationship between class imbalance and machine learning. 

  The review's structure is as follows: an introduction to class imbalance in machine learning, a detailed exploration of its causes and consequences, a comparison of re-sampling techniques, optimization methods, and ensemble learning in the context of class imbalance, an analysis of the relationship between class imbalance and deep learning, and a conclusion that includes recommendations for future research.

The first part of the paper explores the construction of rich word embeddings through a combination of multiple vectors. The publication also discusses the implications of our design choices and the potential for further optimization, highlighting that the type of neural network used for syllable classification does not significantly affect its performance. Additionally, these representations can be applied beyond the specific task of spoken word description, being potentially useful in other speech description tasks such as speech transcription. process of obtaining valuable insights from data remains a significant challenge for many organizations.  A range of data platforms, including Hadoop, Spark, and NoSQL, has been introduced in an attempt to simplify this process, yet managing data systems often still poses a substantial obstacle.  As a result, this study focuses on exploring the potential of Coordinating Agents to facilitate the management of data platforms and their applications.  Here, agents are applied in a data pipeline architecture to evaluate the performance of various approaches and combinations of approaches for data management.  Key among these agents are those responsible for data movement, which involve optimizing the movement of data between different layers of the data pipeline, leveraging either native data platform APIs or alternative, agent-based methods.  Experiments were conducted using both real and synthetic data sets, and the results indicate that the use of data agents can significantly improve data management efficiency and scalability.  Furthermore, this research reveals that the best approach for a particular use case may not be obvious until comparison through experimentation.  As such, a framework for evaluating data management agents and their performance in data pipelines has been established.  This research is innovative in that it applies the concept of data management agents in data pipelines, which has not been extensively explored in the literature.  The findings of this study can be beneficial to organizations in choosing the right data management approach and agents to optimize their data processing operations.  Additionally, the method of evaluating and comparing different data management strategies is also valuable for guiding future research in this domain.  As part of this study, a model for evaluating the effectiveness of data management strategies has been developed.  This model utilizes a set of predefined criteria to assess performance and can be applied to compare agents as well as identify potential areas for improvement.  Key among the criteria for evaluation are agent complexity, scalability, reliability, and cost effectiveness.  Where previous research has focused on using agent-based models to evaluate specific aspects of data management, this study diverges by applying a range of established metrics from the literature to assess the overall performance of data management strategies in data pipelines.  As a result, this research utilizes widely recognized evaluation criteria to gauge the efficacy of data management approaches and identify areas for further exploration.  The ultimate goal of this study is to contribute to the understanding of data management in data pipelines and provide valuable insights for organizations on optimizing their data processing operations.  The methodology of this study involves an experimental design where a range of data management strategies is implemented in data pipelines and their performance is evaluated based on certain criteria. terahertz (THz) radio systems have the potential to significantly enhance wireless data transfer rates, overcoming limited bandwidth in lower-frequency networks.  However, high path loss in these frequency ranges necessitates extensive use of antennas.  Covid-19 restrictions led to reduced mobility and increased dependence on wireless internet, exacerbating antenna shortage.  A novel approach presented here uses machine learning on a mathematical model of mmWave/THz communication to optimize data transfer when antennas are scarce.  Trained models can adapt to varying scenarios without needing complex simulations, and the code for this efficiency-enhancing technique is now open-source for others to use.  Analysis demonstrates that this method achieves near-optimal performance with minimal simplifications, and when combined with other established optimization techniques, it can significantly improve data transfer rates in complex environments.  Further study on system performance can be conducted using the open-source code, which has the added benefit of facilitating efficient resource allocation for mmWave/THz communication with reduced system complexity.  Additionally, the code's ability to efficiently simulate a wide range of scenarios makes it suitable for testing new and innovative wireless access technologies.  A link to the code can be found at https://github.com/stelecom/THz_optimization.  It is worth noting that the code's functionality may experience temporary disruptions due to maintenance; however, efforts will be made to restore accessibility as soon as possible.  All system performance simulations were conducted using the open-source code, which is based on the model presented in [1] and is now available for others to use.  An overview of the techniques utilized for these simulations is as follows.  First, the efficiency of pure beamforming was analyzed, which led to the development of hybrid beamforming, which in turn led to the idea of using reflection to maximize efficiency.  Further refinement of these ideas resulted in the creation of the three core techniques presented here: DeepHyb, DeepRef, and DeepDeepHyb.  DeepHyb combines the best aspects of traditional and hybrid beamforming, which are respectively known as beam-seek and beam-hunt, to maximize data transfer rates.  Reflecting signals to gather more information about the environment can also lead to near-optimal performance. Our ultimate goal is to protect the rights of local communities and promote the ethical use of computer vision technologies. This paper explores the underlying social dynamics that enable the implementation of data governance frameworks in two specific contexts: the West Bank and Kenya. Our research indicates that effective data governance requires the convergence of legal, technical, and social solutions. To this end, we have developed a comprehensive framework, known as the Data Governance Framework for Computer Vision, which comprises principles, policies, and procedures. This paper is pivotal as it marks the first instance where researchers in computer vision address data governance in an systematic manner, drawing from a $5$ year long research journey. Our research highlights that local communities are capable of developing and adhering to data governance frameworks, provided that such initiatives align with their technical and societal needs. This research serves as a model, enabling other institutions to develop their own data governance policies and procedures. Ultimately, our research posits that data governance is a societal issue that exceeds the realm of computer vision, but rather is a broader ethical concern in the world of AI. This research is a call to action, encouraging institutions to prioritize data governance and promote responsible AI practices.   However, WiFi signal strength's instability and directionality complicate measurement. 
  Most current approaches either assume linear relationships between WiFi positions or use nonlinear regression, but without a theoretical foundation. 
  Existing methods also rely on a limited set of training data, assuming sufficient data can linearly or nonlinearly solve for positions. 
  But collecting a sufficient amount of data is impractical due to the needed scale and complexity of mapping. 

  We propose utilizing machine learning regression techniques to build a more stable vehicle positioning system, incorporating external information like road layout and layout maps into the model. 
  Our method leverages a peaking technique to eliminate irrelevant bases and derive a reasonable, limited set of training data. 
  But instead of relying on linear or nonlinear models without a theoretical foundation, we apply a comprehensive model founded on nonconvex optimization. 
  This allows for efficient parameter estimation and adapts to various models including the ones proposed by past researchers. 
  Our method was tested and demonstrated to significantly outperform other methods in constructing the WiFi base field. 
  Moreover, we integrated our method with deep learning and leveraging sparse neural networks, achieved highly accurate localization in a practical scenario, surpassing existing methods by a significant margin. 
  Experimental results suggest that sparse neural solution produces minimal estimation errors and outperforms other methods in both direct estimation and indirect vehicle localization.

Nevertheless, a significant challenge remains in processing tensor-time series data, notably in capturing relationships among tensor elements and across time.  A potential solution is offered by tensor product space-time models that combine tensor product spaces with time-dependent dimensions. This approach is analogous to that used in multivariate time series analysis using space-time AR models. Here, a Bayesian approach is taken to estimating the parameters of these tensor product space-time models.  A Bayesian estimator relies on a stationary distribution, typically provided by an approximate maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate. Two alternative methods are proposed for generating samples from the posterior distribution: one based on a reparameterization trick and a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) method. The proposed sampler is shown to be efficient, with an HMC method outperforming a MAP estimate in both simulated and real-world data sets. An R package has been developed for implementing these methods and is accessible through the link https://github/tensor-space-time-models. This package enables users to model tensor-time series data using the tensor product space-time model. Additionally, it includes functionality for independent component analysis (ICA) and a flexible space-time modeling approach. This package is useful for applications such as signal processing, system identification, and time series forecasting. Furthermore, it allows users to apply tensor product space-time models to data sets involving multiple dimensions, as well as time-dependent elements. The prediction step utilizes the fluid's velocity and time step, while the correction step incorporates the spatial and temporal discretization of the governing equation to ensure consistency. The method has been optimized using a Lagrangian average velocity that eliminates oscillations and excessive dispersal. The optimized tracker has been validated against a established algorithm using a series of academic tests and is ready for use in a wide range of applications. The code can be accessed via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/CPFDResearch/LPCT. The author can be reached at [r.dazinger@imperial.ac.uk](mailto:r.dazinger@imperial.ac.uk). However, using the Tracking-Error Learning method, the optimal point of operation can be continuously adjusted in real-time by modeling the power flow solution through a deep neural network. The approach achieves this by training the network to predict the control variables required to maintain the desired performance variables, such as active and reactive power, when faced with changing loads and other disturbances. Furthermore, the method was found to be more scalable and efficient than other adaptive techniques. The study provides evidence that the Tracking-Error Learning approach can be used to adjust the point of operation to minimize power loss under dynamic conditions. The method's performance on larger systems and in real-world applications is also potentially significant. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the feasibility of applying Tracking-Error Learning to manage the operation of microgrid power systems and achieve improved performance. The $PT$ symmetry, specifically, provides excellent conditions for learning about quantum dynamics within settings of balanced loss and gain.  However, applying this symmetry to real-world situations is challenging due to the need for perfectly balanced loss and gain.  The question then arises of how this symmetry affects systems with imperfect balance.  By using a general quantum-boson model with loss and gain that is not necessarily balanced, we investigate the effect of $PT$ symmetry on quantum dynamics.  We discover that even in an environment with imperfect balance, $PT$ symmetry still produces real Hamiltonians and allows for unitary quantum dynamics.  Furthermore, when the system is in a single-particle state, $PT$ symmetry leads to real energy spectra, real position and momentum wave functions, and real expectation values of any observable.  While an imbalance in loss and gain causes decay in the system's probability density over time, the $PT$-symmetric Hamiltonian remains real.  In fact, the imaginary part of the Hamiltonian that arises due to the imbalance does not contribute to the quantum dynamics.  Finally, when the system is in a two-photon Fock state, $PT$ symmetry in the balanced limit leads to a non-trivial unitary evolution, but in the imperfect balance limit, it results in trivial evolution.  However, for specific applications, such $PT$-invariant states might be attained despite an imbalance in loss and gain.  The study presented here provides insight into the behavior of open quantum systems under $PT$ symmetry in an imperfect balance, which could be useful in experiments.  Additionally, we highlight the utility of $PT$ symmetry in controlling quantum states through mid-span phase modulation.  Based on these findings, we propose a practical method for experimentally achieving $PT$-invariant states in cavities by controlling the pump field.  The study of $PT$ symmetry in quantum dynamics is not only crucial theoretically but also practically.  This study, in particular, provides assistance in designing an experiment for controlling quantum states through mid-span phase modulation.  The application of $PT$ symmetry in quantum systems not only facilitates controlling mid-span phase modulation but also enables novel quantum technologies, such as quantum catalysis, quantum sensing, and quantum metrology. Nevertheless, implementing an encoder-decoder system using eight-bit quantization is challenging. To address this issue, we introduced a innovative reverse conversion tool and proposed an advanced neural speech codec employing eight-bit quantization. Specifically, our codec leverages wavelet transform-based frame-wise separation, followed by the application of eight-bit quantization. Then, a neural post-processing module and a residual learning-based neural decoder are utilized to recover the original speech. Notably, our neural encoder and decoder models can be adapted for both six-bit and eight-bit quantization cases with a single set of parameters. Experimental results demonstrate that the neural codec we designed yields an equivalent quality to the Federal Standard FS1015 codec, which employs six-bit quantization, while achieving better quality than the codec in NEURIPS'19 at a lower bit rate. a critical component in the broader field of image perception.  Standard statistical methods are typically employed to analyze IQA parameters, which are often subjected to hypothesis testing.  While conventional approaches using statistical models are prevalent, they have certain limitations.  A major concern with these methods is the assumption that they must follow specific probability distributions under hypotheses.  A alternative approach to analyzing IQA data uses a non-parametric model called the rank-order model.  This model does not require a predetermined probability distribution and is therefore more versatile.  In this research, we explore the application of the rank-order model in assessing image quality.  A key benefit of this model is that it does not assume a predetermined probability distribution for the data, which is a major limitation of standard statistical methods.  We analyzed various IQA datasets using the rank-order model and compared the results with the findings from hypothesis testing using statistical methods.  A crucial aspect in using the rank-order model is estimating the diversity of the data, which is a challenge.  A new method is proposed to estimate this diversity, which outperformed existing approaches in our experiments.  A key consequence of using the rank-order model is that the conventional P-value is no longer applicable, which forces us to rely on different metrics such as the likelihood ratio and its significance.  In addition to validating the efficacy of the rank-order model, we also investigated its usability through a series of experiments.  A publicly accessible code in Python is also provided to facilitate the replication of our results.  Our analysis reveals that the rank-order model is compatible with standard statistical methods and even outperforms them in terms of their likelihood ratios. Through the utilization of photonic circuits coupled with parametric amplifiers, it is possible to generate and regulate quantum phases of light.  Specifically, this technique has been shown to enhance phase fluctuations in quantum spectroscopy and provide robust protection for quantum phases.  Notably, it has also been explored as an approach for reducing technical noise in quantum systems.  In this study, we examine how this method can be used to modulate an optical field's phase.  We initially investigate how a single SPC configuration affects an input laser field, observing that the field's phase is influenced by its frequency.  This observation leads us to implement a linear frequency modulation (FM) technique to modulate the phase. asks whether it's possible to train a single, general model that can handle a variety of adversarial attacks without needing to be tailored. Our investigation aims to clear up any confusion on this issue and provides a straightforward answer: no, it's not possible to train a general model that can withstand all types of adversarial attacks without model-specific training. However, our research goes beyond simply addressing this query; instead, we look for a constructive solution. We introduce a concept we call 'attack universality,' which means that certain common characteristics of adversarial attacks can be learned from a small dataset of samples. This concept applies not just to a single model but also to its predictions. By encompassing attack universality, we can demonstrate the feasibility of training a general model that can perform well even in the presence of adversarial attacks. To accomplish this, we outline a step-by-step process consisting of two main phases. The first phase involves training a representation model that captures key features from the input while also modeling the inherent adversarial patterns in the data. The second phase uses this representation model to create reliable predictions using robust optimization techniques. Through our implementation based on Certified Adversarial Robustness, we successfully train a general model on CIFAR-10 using approximately 5000 adversarial samples obtained through enumeration. The model we trained achieves a impressive 95.3% accuracy on the adversarial test set, surpassing previous benchmarks in both clean and adversarial environments. The code for our research is available at https://github.com/phasemismatch/universal-aa. Our findings showcase a new path to adversarial robustness through attack universality and highlight the possibility of training a general model using a manageable number of adversarial samples. This model can be used reliably across a variety of adversarial attacks without the need for model-specific fine-tuning. Moreover, we discovered that attack universality has the potential to be extended to other challenges in machine learning, such as handling missing data. The key insight here is that attack universality provides a general framework for modeling complex data by learning from a small set of adversarial samples. This approach can potentially extend to other complex data manipulation techniques not currently covered in this research. Despite this, there has not been significant research into how the Riemann Hypothesis affects quantum dynamics. We investigate this connection by simulating non-Hermitian dynamics based on the Laplacian with a constant complex perturbation in a torus. The quasiperiodic spectrum resulting from this calculation leads to an exponential decay of a corresponding quantum state. The growth rate of this decay is determined by the real part of the perturbation variable, denoted by $b$, and depends on whether the Riemann Hypothesis is assumed to be true or not. Specifically, when the Riemann Hypothesis is assumed, the width of the central peak is shown to be bounded above, leading to long-term nonergodic behavior. On the other hand, when the Riemann Hypothesis is not assumed, the width of the central peak is potentially unbounded as $b$ grows, potentially resulting in ergodic behavior. To validate the Riemann Hypothesis, we simulate a related classical system and numerically verifies that it displays ergodic behavior for all $b$. The ergodicity of this classical system implies that the quantum state should decay according to a power law, contrasting with the long-term nonergodic behavior suggested by assuming the Riemann Hypothesis. We simulate both the ergodic and nonergodic cases numerically, confirming that the ergodic case results in power-law decay of quantum state, while the nonergodic case results in exponentially decay of quantum state. These findings imply that observing ergodic behavior in a deep quantum system would validate the Riemann Hypothesis. Furthermore, we derive an alternative hypothesis that replaces the Riemann Hypothesis and has similar implications for understanding the dynamics of quantum systems. Last but not least, we discuss potential experimental realizations of our model system. The novel features of this model system, particularly the ergodic and nonergodic transitions, could be used to develop innovative quantum measurement techniques and advance our understanding of quantum dynamics. Additionally, we explain how observing a deep quantum system for an extended period of time could potentially validate the Riemann Hypothesis. The complex interplay between quantum, classical, and nonergodicity in this model system could lead to groundbreaking advances in quantum measurement and a deeper understanding of Riemann Hypothesis. However, these waveforms may be affected if the binary's final spin state differs from its initial state due to various physical phenomena such as the migration of the binary in a circumnatal disk. Researchers have discovered that such spin changes can occur even when the binary is not interacting with other materials. A study has been conducted to investigate how a binary's spin changes when it undergoes eccentric mergers at the point where it's closest to the center of a supermassive black hole, a location known as the impact parameter $b$. This study investigates how these temporal patterns can be leveraged to reduce sampling complexity. By focusing on the inter-event times, common statistical methods are adapted and combined to identify significant trends in Twitter's anomaly patterns. Analysis of these patterns around specific events like new software releases or election results indicates lower variability, compared to the inter-event times of unrelated events, suggesting potential opportunities to develop more efficient active learning techniques for identifying rare, challenging-to-classify data points. This concept is illustrated through an example of improving image classification. While this study is conducted on Twitter data, its findings are expected to be universally relevant, opening up new avenues for research. Additionally, the inter-event time analysis is integrated into an information-seeking learning strategy that guides a question-asking process to gain the most informative insights. This approach is tested against a random method and shows promising results in achieving better classification performance. Importantly, the developed techniques are provided as open-source code for reproducibility. This code, along with relevant datasets, can be found at our online repository. This study contributes not only to active learning but also to our understanding of temporal patterns in information dissemination. By examining the inter-event times of our anomalies, new insights into how information spreads on Twitter are obtained. Interestingly, the analysis reveals the presence of human activity, indicating that these patterns are not solely determined by the platform's architecture. Furthermore, the results show that successful information dissemination may be accompanied by periods of decreased activity. This study is based on a part of my PhD thesis, with the full version providing more in-depth details and additional contributions. produced in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Events are selected with at least

charge. Particles are divided into 'trend' and 'tail' groups based on
transverse momentum thresholds of 0.5 and 2 GeV per charge, used to define the

behavior in small-system collisions, with results displayed as raw two-dimensional
scans, corrected for instrumental influences, revealing an evident short-range
anisotropy. The measured correlations show a notable excess in the lower
transverse momentum region, thought to stem from epicyclic flow. Additionally, the
study explores correlations using track-like particles, incorporating data from
both the silicon pixel detector. The si pixel detector was found to introduce a
small bias in the lower transverse momentum range but had a minimal impact in the
high transverse momentum region. The analysis also examines the stability of the
corrections applied to the data, finding these to be resilient against changes in
event yield and distribution. Lastly, the study compares its results with model
predictions from a hydrodynamical model, showcasing its ability to account for
anisotropy observed within the trend region while falling short in explaining the
anisotropy observed within the tail region. The analysis remains sensitive to variations
in the length of the system. The study also highlights that a modified version of
the hydrodynamical model, incorporating an initial condition generator based on
central and peripheral collisions, can adequately explain anisotropy observed in
both the trend and tail regions. However, the model requires an increased system

higher centre-of-mass energy could help reduce data to be better explained by the

two-dimensional scans, alongside tables detailing the findings. The study is

The particles interact in a way that causes them to move towards regions with the lowest population count. We demonstrate both numerically and analytically that in these systems, higher system complexity can be achieved by introducing non-uniform particle distributions, where we observe a significant increase in complexity for small system sizes and a notable increase for larger sizes, amounting to up to 30% in our data. We found that this increase in complexity is a result of both the particles' spatial arrangement and their individual states. Additionally, we found that this effect is influenced by the specific interaction rule the particles follow. We found that when the particles' interaction is minimal, the complexity increases uniformly, but when their interaction is stronger, this increase is accompanied by a significant drop in entropy and the emergence of two distinct particle populations with varying states.   demonstrates that the risk associated with sequencing can lead to a

This diabatic transition leverages the non-reciprocity introduced by an asymmetric waveguide and can be controlled with an adjacent microwave beam. By integrating this adiabatic process into a dark qubit system, we establish a means for efficiently and rapidly turning dark qubit operations on and off. By employing a strategy of point-counting on curves, we establish upper bounds for the colored absolute discriminant based on the absolute discriminant of a related lower-degree curve.  These results lead to a significant improvement in the colored absolute discriminant for curves with high genus.  Additionally, we prove that for certain special types of curves - those defined over a finite field and having a specific type of singularity - the colored absolute discriminant is represented by a particular quadratic form, which also provides new lower bounds.  These results combine to give the most accurate estimates yet for certain types of rational function fields and their colored absolute discriminants.  Finally, we apply these findings to derive new bounds on the Weil's absolute discriminant of a certain class of function fields, which were previously established by Borel and later refined by Borel and Chowla.  In a separate direction, we explore a long-standing conjecture related to the general form of a degree-$n$ polynomial, which has additional significance in the study of function fields, although this aspect is not directly addressed in the paper.  It's worth noting that the approaches used here were influenced by earlier works of Bateman, Erdos, Manin, and Poonvalu-Seo but have distinctively new methodological contributions.  In particular, the second author's new point-counting technique, which was previously weakly implied in [arXiv:2105.07124], now explicitly gives rise to the current results, which also provide new perspectives on recent works in the field.  It's also worth noting that the first co-author's initial thoughts on the current research were first shared in a personal message to [arXiv:2105.07124], which further highlighted the current combined results.  While the approaches used here were partially influenced by prior works, the current research is considered to be an important new contribution to the field.  It's also worth noting that the techniques and findings of this paper may be applied to solve the long-standing conjecture related to the general form of a degree-$n$ polynomial, which is outside the scope of the current paper but is planned to be addressed in a future work.  Furthermore, the methods of this paper can be used to extend the existing bounds on certain types of rational function fields, which was also outside the scope of the current paper but is planned to be addressed in a future work.

In this paper, we explore a secure data-sharing cooperation process, where agents make regular data-sharing choices with a focus on their long-term benefits.  We examine a variety of security risks, including unverified data exposure and contamination, and create an iterative prisoner's dilemma game to model an agent's decision to share data.  We also develop an approach to balance reward and security in data-sharing cooperation through the implementation of a Bayesian game.  We find that situations with a common goal among agents and when those agents are relatively strong in terms of trust and verifiable capabilities improve data-sharing cooperation.  We ultimately consider a distribution of private values that reflects the varying levels of benefit that agents derive from their data, resulting in a cooperative data-sharing dynamic where more verifiable agents tend to contribute more.  We test our findings in the context of a real-world cooperative data-sharing experiment involving vehicle manufacturers and service centers and find that results align with our theoretical predictions.  We conclude with discussions on potential future research topics. A common approach in addresssing this issue involves using epigraphic loss functions that incorporate the performance of previous tasks into the optimization of current models. Despite the conceptual and mathematical connections between epigraphic loss and multi-objective optimization, the theoretical underpinnings of epigraphic learning remain unclear. Furthermore, prior studies have not adequately regulated the model updates in a theoretically sound manner. This work provides a definitive analysis of the theoretical framework underlying epigraphic learning, involving the optimization of a decreasing hyperplane that is adapted based on past tasks. Our investigation of a wide array of epigraphic loss functions reveals that their performance is regulated by specific properties of the stream of tasks. A critical aspect of our research involves the design of an explicit training procedure that maximally leverages past task information while regulating model updates in an environmentally friendly way. We also conduct thorough evaluations of prominent continual learning methods that employ epigraphic loss functions, finding that many of these techniques lack theoretical justifications. This study provides a comprehensive framework for the design of efficient epigraphic loss functions and corresponding training algorithms, which we validate through extensive empirical tests on well-known continual learning benchmarks. Interestingly, our results reveal that epigraphic learning is capable of successfully accommodating tasks with both simple and complex data distribution transformations. All the code and supporting evidence are available at: https://github.com/alexeyvora/epigraphic-continual-learning. a single infected individual in a well-mixed population is often taken as the basic reproduction number in epidemiological models, which is typically determined through statistical analysis of epidemic data. In this study, a novel approach using Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation is presented for directly estimating the basic reproduction number from cumulative incidence and reporting rates. The proposed method is demonstrated to be accurate and efficient, even in scenarios where reporting rates vary among groups and data are not available for specific time periods. Furthermore, we modify this approach to account for changes in reporting rates and apply it to two real-world datasets, one from Maine, USA, and the other from Victoria, Australia, both relating to COVID-19 cases. The results of these analyses are compared with the traditional epidemiological estimates for each dataset. The implementation of our method is provided in R, which can be accessed via the link https://github.com/lucamonti/est_R0. The script assumes that reporting rates are constant over time and do not change, although variations in reporting rates can also be accounted for. Additionally, assuming that cases are independently reported is another underlying condition of this approach. If a person contracts multiple cases close to each other in time, these infections may not be separately reported, which could lead to an underestimation of the basic reproduction number. Despite these limitations, we believe that the presented method can provide a simple and accurate way to estimate the basic reproduction number in epidemiological contexts.

  \textbf{GalRotpy} is a Python package that offers tools for analyzing data from circularly rotating galactic potentials. 
  GalRotpy is built on top of the Telescopic Redshift Surface technique, enabling the computation of circular velocity curves. 
  It also includes tools for analyzing associated metrics like the transverse force curve and the $m$-derivative of the circular velocity curve. 
  GalRotpy is designed to be versatile and can be employed in both observational studies of the Galaxy and simulations of galactic models. 
  A case study is provided in the package as an example of its capabilities. 
  The code is documented and hosted on the Galactic Hub at \url{https://galactic-hub.org}, with its repository located at \url{https://github.com/GRH-RR/GalRotPy}.

one of the most popular AI techniques for operating on graph structures, with extensive applications in forecasting user behavior, material properties, and environmental management, among other areas.  The vast majority of GNN research has focused on training models, with little regard for model efficiency once trained.  Our study invests in developing post-training efficiency enhancements for GNN models, drawing on lessons from modern optimization and networking disciplines.  The ease of shifting GNN training to graph data and back to a physical graph, as well as the need for real-time model accessibility, presents significant challenges to direct model deployment.  In response, we develop a novel distributed graph splitting and acceleration strategy, combining it with dynamic pruning to create a two-stage process.  Each stage employs a custom graph structure, with the splitting process using a graph partitioning algorithm based on node importance, and the acceleration process employing a message-passing algorithm informed by optimal transport principles.  Our approach, when applied to various GNN models and datasets, yields significant reductions in computational cost and memory usage, outperforming alternative methods while maintaining accuracy at or near original model performance. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by developing a novel method to identify plagiarism across languages. Weighing matrices can be obtained by taking a particular linear combination of two specific types of symmetric matrices.  Our proposed method involves first creating a weakly symmetric idempotent matrix and then finding a suitable permutation of squares for its transformation, ultimately yielding a set of weighing matrices in the process.  This method is flexible and can be used to generate a wide range of non-existent weighing matrices for certain parameters, while also providing an alternative method for constructing existing weighing matrices.  Specifically, we employ this method to create non-existent weighing matrices for parameters $(7, 21, 8, 3)$ and $(21, 63, 16)$, while also re-determining existing weighing matrices for parameters $(15, 63, 8)$ and $(33, 99, 8)$.  This method employs a linear representation of weakly symmetric idempotent matrices and has the added benefit of facilitating the exploration of linear groups associated with these matrices.  Furthermore, we observe that the property of a matrix being weakly symmetric idempotent is preserved under the action of certain linear groups, which leads to an interesting question regarding the existence of prime divisors for certain quantities derived from these matrices.  Additionally, we provide a list of linear groups associated with certain known weighing matrices, while also illustrating an example of how our method can be used to create a family of weakly symmetric idempotent matrices and their corresponding weighing matrices for an arbitrary number of parameters $q$.  This example particularly shows that our method can be employed to generate non-existent weighing matrices for parameters $(q, q^2 + 1, q)$ for any arbitrary prime number $q$.  Lastly, we extend an existing approach by Bruckner and Nebe for calculating the central linear group for a specific type of quadratic form, while also providing an example of a non-existent quadratic form with a central linear group for parameters $(7, 21, 8)$ and further imply a newly defined theorem regarding the non-existence of weakly symmetric idempotent matrices for certain parameters based on Bruckner and Nebe's work. The standard LDG formulation relies on flux-form discretization which poses significant challenges despite its scalability. The primary issue arises from the non-symmetric diffusion-term and the presence of gravity in the equation. The latter causes the diagonal entries of the Galerkin matrix to become unstable and dependent on the finite element space, thus precluding the use of standard stability analysis. To overcome these limitations, we derive sharp a priori error estimates for LDG with gravity, which demonstrate the independence of the errors from the finite element space. The errors are shown to converge at the same rate as in gravity-free cases. All findings are substantiated through a series of numerical experiments. The agent's goal is to learn a sequence of optimal actions that maximizes the expected cumulative reward relative to a reference policy designed by an ideal designer. We investigate the performance of standard exploration algorithms in the context of these environmental parameters. in an ensemble of three-level atoms, mediated by a laser beam, whose phase is manipulated dynamically.  The phase transition is characterized by a sharp decline in the bulk quantum purity of the system and is marked by a non-uniform distribution of the entanglement across the atomic ensemble.  Notably, the quantum phase transition is induced not by a change in the drive parameters but by the diffusion of entropic information within the system.  Our results indicate that this diffusion plays a critical role in the collapse of local purity in the ensemble's sub-systems, resulting in a significant decrease in the overall quantum purity of the system as the phase of the laser beam is altered.  We substantiate these claims through numerical simulations conducted on an atomic ensemble and validate them against theoretical calculations based on the entanglement density and phase transition theory.  Our research thus provides the first direct evidence of a quantum phase transition induced through entropic information diffusion in an ensemble of three-level atoms.  We further expand on this finding, proposing a two-dimensional phase diagram for the quantum phase transition, based on both atomic and photonic components, and exploring the potential of this diffusion to create complex entangled states in atomic ensembles.  Our work opens up new avenues for understanding quantum phase transitions in complex systems and perhaps even harnessing them for information technology applications.  We demonstrate that these transitions can be optimized and controlled by adjusting laser beam parameters and implementing coherent atomic elimination, thereby creating a platform for manipulating quantum states in atomic ensembles.  We also identify and characterize the points of emergence for three-level entanglement and symmetric states in this system, supported by numerical simulations and theoretical calculations.  Our research thus provides a comprehensive framework and set of tools for creating and controlling quantum states in atomic ensembles, leveraging complex entangled phases and points of emergence.  We showcase the capability of generating three-body entanglement by adjusting laser beam parameters and implementing coherent atomic elimination, and explain how this entanglement arises from the interplay of atomic and photonic components.  We also illustrate the potential of generating entropic information phases by controlling laser beam frequency and strength, and suggest ways to create and observe these phases.  Our work describes a versatile laboratory for exploring and controlling complex entangled phases, points of emergence, and entropic information phases in three-level ensembles, adaptable to a range of experimental setups.  We demonstrate that these phases can be optimized and controlled by adjusting atomic and photonic components, and leverage this control to create a range of complex entangled states.
